Captain Ernest Alfred Johnson

Biography

Introduction: The Seafaring Ethos of Saba

The maritime history of the Caribbean is populated by legendary navigators whose lives read like epic adventure novels, yet few embody the courage, mystical intuition, and technical mastery of Saban seamanship quite like Captain Ernest Alfred Johnson. Born on an island that possessed no natural harbor and required its people to launch boats through pounding surf from rocky shores, Johnson was destined for the sea. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, Saba produced an extraordinary generation of master mariners who navigated the world's oceans with unmatched skill. Among them, Ernest Alfred Johnson—widely celebrated in maritime lore as "21 Knot Johnson" and affectionately known locally as "Freddie"—rose from humble beginnings as a teenage sailor to become a revered ship commander, a hero of maritime rescue, and a prolific chronicler of West Indian seafaring life. His career bridged the romantic era of working sail and the modern age of steam propulsion, leaving an indelible mark on the maritime heritage of the Netherlands Antilles.

Early Life and Ascent from Donkeyman to Master Mariner

Ernest Alfred Johnson was born on June 15, 1884, on the island of Saba, to William James Johnson and Judith Eleanor Dowling. Growing up in the picturesque village of Windwardside beneath the imposing slopes of Mount Scenery, young Ernest was captivated by the tales of returning sea captains who brought home goods, currencies, and stories from global ports. Like most young Saban men of his generation, his formal classroom education was abbreviated in favor of practical seafaring apprenticeship. Around the year 1900, at the tender age of sixteen, Johnson bade farewell to his family and embarked on his first deep-water voyage, entering the harsh and demanding world of international merchant shipping.

Johnson’s ascent through the maritime ranks was characterized by relentless hard work, physical endurance, and a keen analytical mind. He began his service in the grueling lower decks of sailing vessels and early steamships, working as a "donkeyman"—the crew member responsible for operating and maintaining the auxiliary steam engines (donkey engines) used for hoisting anchor chains and cargo handling. This difficult, grease-stained labor provided him with an intimate mechanical knowledge of ship operations that would prove invaluable in his later career as a steamship captain. Through unwavering determination and self-directed study in navigation, meteorology, and maritime law during long sea watches, Johnson steadily earned his promotions, achieving his mate's qualifications before successfully passing the rigorous examinations to earn his Master Mariner's license. In 1906, solidifying his roots in his island community despite his global travels, he married Mary Ellen Hassell, with whom he built an enduring family legacy.

The Nickname: "21 Knot Johnson" and Caribbean Navigation

Throughout the maritime communities of the West Indies and the eastern seaboard of the United States, Captain Johnson became universally known by the colorful sobriquet "21 Knot Johnson". The nickname was born out of his reputation for extraordinary speed, fearlessness in carrying sail, and an aggressive, highly efficient approach to vessel management. Whether commanding traditional wooden schooners or modern steel-hulled steamers, Johnson was renowned for pushing his vessels to their absolute operational limits without compromising crew safety or structural integrity.

"Known across the ports of the West Indies and the Eastern Seaboard as '21 Knot Johnson,' his life embodied the golden age of Saban seamanship and heroic maritime rescue."

His navigational expertise was particularly evident during trade runs between the Windward Islands, Curaçao, and North American ports. In an era when tropical weather forecasting relied heavily on barometric readings and visual observation of sea states, Johnson demonstrated an uncanny ability to navigate around destructive hurricanes and maximize prevailing trade winds. His peers often marveled at his fast transit times, which allowed his vessels to secure premium freight rates and beat competitors to market. He worked closely alongside other notable Saban maritime figures, including Captain Thomas Charles Vanterpool, contributing to the collective reputation of Saban captains as the most reliable and capable navigators in the Caribbean basin.

The Miracle Rescue of the Submarine USS S-5

While Captain Johnson’s career was filled with remarkable voyages, his name was etched into international maritime history on September 2, 1920, through a rescue operation that combined dramatic heroism with unexplained maritime intuition. At the time, Johnson was commanding the coastal steamer SS Alanthus (often recorded in contemporary press as Atlanthus), sailing along the Atlantic coast of the United States toward Boston. The vessel was proceeding along its standard commercial route when Captain Johnson experienced a profound, unexplainable premonition—a persistent internal conviction that he needed to deviate from his established shipping lane.

"Something told me to change course. It wasn't logic or routine; it was the instinct of a seaman who knows that the ocean speaks to those willing to listen."

Yielding to this powerful intuition, Johnson ordered his helmsman to alter course into an unfrequented stretch of ocean off the coast of Delaware. Shortly after the deviation, the lookout aboard the Alanthus spotted an unusual object protruding from the oceanic swells: the tail and rudder post of a submarine, tilted vertically towards the sky, with a makeshift white flag fluttering from a copper tube. It was the United States Navy submarine USS S-5, which had suffered a catastrophic valve failure during a dive trial, causing its forward compartments to flood and trapping nearly forty officers and men inside the suffocating, darkened hull.

Demonstrating consummate seamanship, Captain Johnson expertly maneuvered the bulky steamer Alanthus directly alongside the bobbing stern of the submarine in open water. He ordered heavy steel cables, chains, and manila hawsers wrapped around the submarine's exposed hull, securing it firmly to the steamer to prevent it from plunging into the oceanic depths. Recognizing that the trapped crew was running out of oxygen, Johnson directed his ship’s engineers to construct a wooden work platform over the water and rig an improvised air hose from the steamer's pumps, forcing fresh air through a small drill hole into the submarine. Furthermore, using his ship's communications, he flagged down the larger passenger steamer SS General George W. Goethals, coordinating naval radio SOS signals that brought U.S. Navy destroyers and rescue ships rushing to the scene. Thanks to Captain Johnson’s miraculous course deviation, technical ingenuity, and leadership, every single crew member of the USS S-5 was saved from certain death—an achievement that brought Johnson widespread national acclaim and commendations from naval authorities.

Booby Hill Residence and Retirement in Saba

Despite his extensive travels across global oceans and long residences in American maritime hubs, Captain Johnson’s heart remained inextricably bound to his native Saba. In 1906, utilizing wealth generated from his maritime commands, he imported high-quality lumber and building supplies directly from New York to construct a magnificent family residence situated on Booby Hill. Perched high above the Caribbean Sea, the home offered panoramic vistas of the surrounding ocean, allowing the veteran captain to observe passing vessels and weather patterns much as he had from the bridge of his ships.

Upon retiring from active sea duty, Captain Johnson returned permanently to his Booby Hill estate, becoming a revered civic figure and elder statesman within the Saban community. His home became a gathering place for younger sailors seeking advice on navigation, maritime employment, and international shipping lanes. He served as an informal harbor advisor and mentor, helping to maintain Saba's maritime traditions during a period when the island's economy was beginning to diversify away from purely seafaring pursuits. His presence provided a tangible link to the golden age of sail and early steam navigation.

Literary Legacy: The Unpublished Manuscript and Historical Impact

Perhaps Captain Johnson’s most unique contribution to Caribbean history was his prolific written documentation of early twentieth-century seafaring life. During his retirement years on Booby Hill, he dedicated himself to writing extensive memoirs chronicling his maritime adventures, shipwrecks, rescues, and observations of West Indian culture. He was extensively interviewed by Dr. Goslinga, the Dutch Inspector of Education, resulting in a monumental manuscript titled "21 Knot Johnson: Life and Adventures".

Though this remarkable memoir remained unpublished during his lifetime, it circulated widely in manuscript form among historians and scholars. Prominent Antillean author and intellectual Frank Martinus Arion recognized the immense historical value of Johnson's writings, advocating passionately for their preservation and recognition as primary literary artifacts of Caribbean working-class history. In modern times, celebrated Saban historian and author Will Johnson has extensively researched and popularized Captain Johnson’s exploits, incorporating his narratives into seminal books such as Tales from My Grandmother’s Pipe and numerous historical essays on The Saba Islander. Today, Captain Ernest Alfred Johnson is permanently commemorated at Juliana's Hotel on Saba, where one of the exclusive "Captains' Suites" bears his name and displays his remarkable story, ensuring that the legacy of "21 Knot Johnson" continues to inspire generations of seafarers and historians alike.

Major Contributions

  • Captain Ernest Alfred 'Freddie' Johnson, internationally celebrated as '21 Knot Johnson,' made extraordinary contributions to West Indian maritime navigation, emergency rescue, and historical documentation.
  • Rising from donkeyman to master mariner, he established a reputation for elite vessel management and speed across complex Caribbean and Atlantic trade routes.
  • His most famous achievement occurred on September 2, 1920, when his intuitive course deviation and brilliant technical seamanship aboard the SS Alanthus enabled the rescue of nearly forty trapped crew members from the sunken U.
  • S.
  • Navy submarine USS S-5 off the Delaware coast.
  • Additionally, his prolific autobiographical memoirs preserved an irreplaceable primary record of Saban seafaring heritage, inspiring regional historians and cementing Saba's reputation as a premier cradle of Caribbean seamanship.
